## Detection and Isolation of Sensor Attacks for Autonomous Vehicles

Research investigates the cyber-security problem for autonomous vehicles under sensor attacks, proposing a model-based framework which can detect sensor attacks and identify their sources in order to achieve the secure localization of self-driving vehicles.

### Technical Approach

A bank of attack detectors is developed to capture anomalies in each sensor measurement, which is a combination of an extended Kalman filter (EKF) and a cumulative sum (CUSUM) discriminator. EKFs are employed to estimate the vehicle position and orientation recursively, while each CUSUM discriminator is designed to analyze the residual generated by its combined EKF to detect the possible deviation of the sensor measurement from the expected pose derived according to the mathematical model of the vehicle.

### Redundancy and Sensor Fusion

To ensure robustness of the vehicle against cyber-attacks, sensor redundancy is introduced, that is to deploy multiple sensors, each of which provides real-time pose observations of the vehicle.

## SAVIOR: Securing Autonomous Vehicles with Robust Physical Invariants

The paper was authored by Raul Quinonez (University of Texas at Dallas), Jairo Giraldo (University of Utah), Luis Salazar (University of California, Santa Cruz), Erick Bauman (University of Texas at Dallas), Alvaro Cardenas (University of California, Santa Cruz), and Zhiqiang Lin (Ohio State University). It was presented at the 29th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 20) in 2020.

**Overview:**
The paper addresses how autonomous vehicles tend to trust sensor information without data validation or verification, allowing attackers to exploit these limitations by feeding erroneous sensor data. SAVIOR is an architecture for securing autonomous vehicles with robust physical invariants, implemented and validated on two popular open-source controllers for aerial and ground vehicles.

I've found relevant research on adversarial robustness in autonomous driving systems. Here's a summary of the key findings:

## Stealthy Attacks in Autonomous Driving

Recent work proposes stealthy and more effective optimization-based attack methods by reformulating the optimization problem using Lagrangian relaxation and designing a Frenet-based objective function along with distinct constraint space. Researchers have introduced optical adversarial examples where perturbations are created using shadows to carry out natural and stealthy physical-world adversarial attacks under a black-box setting.

## Multi-Sensor Fusion Vulnerabilities

Studies analyzing high-performance sensor fusion models found them vulnerable to purposefully crafted image-based adversarial attacks including disappearance, universal patch, and spoofing despite using LIDAR sensors. One attack achieves over 90% success rate across different object types and multi-sensor fusion algorithms and is found stealthy, robust to victim positions, transferable across MSF algorithms, and physical-world realizable.

## GNSS/Localization Security

A sensor fusion-based GNSS spoofing attack detection framework for autonomous vehicles uses comparison between predicted location shift and inertial sensor based location shift in addition to monitoring vehicle motion states. Recent work proposes novel attack strategies leveraging constrained optimization techniques to minimize the energy required to achieve specific attack objectives against localization systems.

## Dynamic and Physical Attacks

Novel adversarial attack approaches enable patches not co-located with targets for more versatile and stealthy attacks, utilizing dynamic patches displayed on screens allowing for adaptive changes and movement.

The search results reveal significant research from 2022-2023 addressing the intersection of attack budgets, stealthiness, sensor fusion, and localization in autonomous driving security.

I found relevant research on malicious attacks against multi-sensor fusion systems in autonomous driving. Here are the key findings:

## Recent Security Research (2023-2024)

Autonomous driving vehicles rely on various sensor data for perception and localization, and attackers can forge sensor data to interfere with the autonomous system's estimation of the vehicle's current state, thereby posing a threat to vehicle safety.

### Multi-Sensor Fusion Architecture

Multi-sensor fusion systems combine position information from GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System), position and orientation data from LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging), and inertial estimates from IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) to provide accurate state estimations such as position, velocity, and orientation.

### Attack Methods and Vulnerabilities

Existing research addresses sensor spoofing across IMU, LiDAR, and GPS systems. A significant study from November 2024 presents "a comprehensive security analysis of Error-State Kalman Filter (ESKF) based multi-sensor fusion systems for autonomous driving, addressing a critical gap in the existing literature."

The research introduces a novel error analysis model specifically designed for ESKF-based localization systems, revealing that errors can be represented as a linear combination of injected signals under steady-state conditions.

### Real-World Attack Demonstrations

Recent 2024 research demonstrates practical attacks on autonomous driving systems: Success rates in off-road attack scenarios increased from 59.5% to 82%, while wrong-way attacks rose from 45.5% to 73.5%, with off-road attacks completing in an average of 16.6 seconds.

The search results show this is an active area of security research with multiple papers published in 2023-2024 focusing on the vulnerabilities of multi-sensor fusion localization systems in autonomous vehicles.

## Key Finding: "Drift with Devil" (2020)

A 2020 USENIX Security paper titled "Drift with Devil: Security of multi-sensor fusion based localization in high-level autonomous driving under GPS spoofing" addresses combined localization attacks involving GPS spoofing.

## Related LiDAR Spoofing Research

There are also several related works on fooling LiDAR detection models:

1. **Adversarial LiDAR Attacks**: Research explores the possibility of strategically controlling spoofed points to fool machine learning models in the object detection step.

2. **Trajectory-Based Attacks**: One approach reveals a danger of spoofing the trajectory to attack deep modules through the LiDAR motion correction process without any need of software hacking. GPS jamming or spoofing can be used to arbitrarily modify GPS trajectory, and when GNSS and INS are fused, such attacks can affect not only positions but also the rotational component of a vehicle's trajectory.

3. **Defense Mechanisms**: A defense study proposes CARLO to mitigate LiDAR spoofing attacks by detecting spoofed data through treating ignored occlusion patterns as invariant physical features, which reduces the mean attack success rate to 5.5%.

The search results indicate active research in this area combining LiDAR and GPS attacks against autonomous vehicle localization and perception systems.

**Title:** Ghost Navigator: How Silent Positioning Attacks Target Autonomous Vehicles

**Authors & Year:** Not clearly visible in the PDF header provided

## Key Contributions

The research introduces a novel attack methodology that extends beyond traditional GNSS spoofing by simultaneously targeting multiple sensor systems used in autonomous vehicle navigation.

## Ghost Navigator Attack Overview

The Ghost Navigator attack represents an advancement in positioning system compromise. Rather than attacking GPS/GNSS signals alone, it "targets multiple sensors including inertial measurement units and odometry" to create coordinated false positioning data.

## Sensors Targeted

The attack focuses on:
- GNSS/GPS receivers
- Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs)
- Odometry systems

## Differentiation from Prior Work

Previous attacks concentrated on GNSS spoofing exclusively. Ghost Navigator distinguishes itself by creating a "multi-sensor fusion attack" that exploits how autonomous vehicles integrate data from multiple positioning sources, making the false navigation signals more difficult to detect and validate.

## Attack Model

The methodology demonstrates how attackers can manipulate sensor data simultaneously to maintain consistency across the vehicle's integrated navigation stack, bypassing defenses designed for single-sensor attacks.

I've successfully found comprehensive information about the "Drift with Devil" paper. Here's a summary of the search results:

## Overview

"Drift with Devil: Security of Multi-Sensor Fusion based Localization in High-Level Autonomous Driving under GPS Spoofing" was published at the 29th USENIX Security Symposium in 2020 by researchers from UC Irvine.

## Research Focus

The research addresses localization security in high-level autonomous vehicles, filling a critical gap by studying whether multi-sensor fusion algorithms are sufficiently secure under GPS spoofing in autonomous vehicle settings.

## Key Findings

The researchers identify two AV-specific attack goals (off-road and wrong-way attacks) and discover a "take-over effect" that can fundamentally defeat the multi-sensor fusion design principle.

They design FusionRipper, a novel and general attack that opportunistically captures and exploits take-over vulnerabilities and is highly robust to practical factors such as spoofing inaccuracies.

## Evaluation Results

FusionRipper was evaluated on 6 real-world sensor traces and achieved at least 97% and 91.3% success rates for off-road and wrong-way attacks respectively. Under normal error amounts, the success rate was reduced by only 0.2% for off-road attacks and 0.8% for wrong-way attacks, and even at 3x error amounts, success rates remained at 84.3% and 74.2% respectively.

Based on the search results, here are the key findings related to reinforcement learning, sensor injection attacks, EKF state estimation in cyber-physical systems:

## Key Research Areas

**False Data Injection Attacks (FDIA) Detection:**
EKF and UKF are adopted for dynamic state estimation in detecting false data injection attacks in smart grids and cyber-physical systems. When attacked by FDIAs, results of different state estimation methods produce significant differences, with the static method deviating from the true state, while the dynamic method is closer to the true state due to prediction steps.

**Reinforcement Learning-Based Detection:**
The online attack detection problem is formulated as a partially observable Markov decision process problem with a detector for each sensor based on model-free reinforcement learning. Detectors are designed for each sensor based on the framework of model-free reinforcement learning.

**Cyber-Physical System Security with RL:**
The optimal policy selection problem of attacker and sensor in cyber-physical systems under DoS attacks uses a two-player zero-sum game with Nash equilibrium strategies, and a reinforcement learning algorithm is proposed to dynamically adjust the corresponding strategies.

**PPO and Deep Reinforcement Learning:**
Recent work mentions deep reinforcement learning (DRL) employed to design automatic detection against false data injection attacks on cyber-physical systems, with PPO recognized for its off-policy learning and stable convergence fidelity.

**Actuator Attacks on Autonomous Vehicles:**
An extended Kalman filter (EKF) is employed for state estimation and to monitor attack residues, assisting in creating an efficient attack detection mechanism.

The research spans 2021-2023 with applications to smart grids, power systems, and autonomous vehicles.

I found relevant research on optimal actuator and sensor attacks on autonomous vehicles using reinforcement learning. Here's a summary of the key findings:

## Primary Research

A reinforcement learning (RL)-based approach has been proposed for designing optimal stealthy integrity attacks on autonomous vehicle (AV) actuators. This novel learning-based method is designed to create optimal stealthy actuator attacks on autonomous vehicles.

## Key Focus Areas

A key focus is on the stealthiness of attacks, which is crucial given that modern autonomous vehicle systems are equipped with advanced attack detectors. The research investigates the vulnerability of autonomous vehicles to stealthy actuator attacks, focusing on false data injection (FDI) attacks.

## Defense and Limitations

The research also analyzes the limitations of state-of-the-art RL-based secure controllers developed to counter such attacks. The design of secure controllers based on specific FDI attacks and training data obtained through RL has limitations, as it restricts generalization to different types of attacks.

## Related Work on Sensor Attacks

Beyond actuator attacks, an adversarial agent has been trained online to generate optimal adversarial attacks on observations, which attempts to amplify the average variation distance on perturbed policies. Research demonstrates that adversarial attacks with trained adversarial agents have distinct impacts on driving safety, with collision times increasing significantly compared to cases without attacks.

The research combines advanced reinforcement learning techniques with cyber-physical security to understand and model threats to autonomous vehicle systems.

Based on the search results, I found relevant research on generating adversarial driving scenarios for autonomous vehicles. Here's what I found:

## Abeysirigoonawardena 2019 Research

Yasasa Abeysirigoonawardena published "Generating Adversarial Driving Scenarios in High-Fidelity Simulators" in May 2019. The paper proposes using Bayesian optimization to generate adversarial self-driving scenarios that expose poorly-engineered or poorly-trained self-driving policies, and increase the risk of collision with simulated pedestrians and vehicles.

## Key Approach and Optimization

The paper proposes to automate the process using Bayesian optimization to generate adversarial self-driving scenarios that expose poorly-engineered or poorly-trained self-driving policies. The work proposes to automatically generate difficult scenarios in urban environments, by learning the placements of pedestrians such that the induced scenarios are highly challenging for a given autonomous vehicle.

## Training and Safety Improvements

By incorporating the generated scenarios into the training set of the self-driving policy, and by fine-tuning the policy using vision-based imitation learning, safer self-driving behavior is obtained.

## Related Work

It's worth noting that Abeysirigoonawardena has also published subsequent work on this topic. A later method efficiently generates adversarial simulation scenarios for autonomous driving by solving an optimal control problem that aims to maximally perturb the policy from its nominal trajectory, which demonstrates the continuation of this research area.

I found comprehensive information about the Boloor 2020 paper on attacking vision-based perception in autonomous driving. Here are the key findings:

## Paper Overview

The paper presents novel end-to-end attacks on autonomous driving in simulation, using simple physically realizable attacks: the painting of black lines on the road, targeting deep neural network models for end-to-end autonomous driving control.

## Attack Methodology

The research systematically studies the painting of black lines on the road, which are unsuspicious since they are semantically inconsequential (few human drivers would be confused) and are similar to common imperfections observed in the real world, such as skid marks or construction markers.

## Key Findings and Techniques

A systematic investigation shows that such attacks are easy to engineer, and the research describes scenarios in which they are highly effective, defining several objective functions that quantify the success of an attack and developing techniques based on Bayesian Optimization to efficiently traverse the search space of higher dimensional attacks.

The research defines a novel class of hijacking attacks, where painted lines on the road cause the driverless car to follow a target path.

Through the use of network deconvolution, the research provides insights into the successful attacks, which appear to work by mimicking activations of entirely different scenarios.

## Authors and Publication

The paper was authored by Adith Boloor, Karthik Garimella, Xin He, Christopher Gill, Yevgeniy Vorobeychik, and Xuan Zhang. The 2020 publication appeared in the Journal of Systems Architecture, volume 110:101766.

I found comprehensive information about the paper you're looking for. Here are the key details:

## Paper Overview

"Drift with Devil: Security of Multi-Sensor Fusion based Localization in High-Level Autonomous Driving under GPS Spoofing" was presented at the 29th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 20) in 2020 by Junjie Shen, Jun Yeon Won, Zeyuan Chen, and Qi Alfred Chen.

## Main Findings

The research identifies two AV-specific attack goals: off-road and wrong-way attacks. The researchers discovered a take-over effect that can fundamentally defeat the MSF design principle.

## Attack Method

The researchers designed FusionRipper, a novel and general attack that opportunistically captures and exploits take-over vulnerabilities, achieving ≥97% and 91.3% success rates for off-road and wrong-way attacks respectively, with high robustness to practical factors such as spoofing inaccuracies.

## Vulnerability Discovery

The analysis showed that when the MSF is in relatively unconfident periods due to dynamic and non-deterministic real-world factors such as sensor noises and algorithm inaccuracies, GPS spoofing is able to cause exponential growths of deviations in the MSF output.

## Evaluation

The researchers used the ba-local trace collected by the Apollo team, which is designed specifically for evaluating MSF-based localization algorithms for Apollo.

## Main Research on Sensor Fusion-based GNSS Spoofing Detection

A sensor fusion-based GNSS spoofing attack detection framework for autonomous vehicles consists of two strategies: (i) comparison between predicted location shift and inertial sensor based location shift in addition to monitoring of vehicle motion states (standstill/in motion); and (ii) detection and classification of turns (left or right) along with detection of vehicle motion states.

In the first strategy, data from low-cost in-vehicle inertial sensors—speedometer, accelerometer, and steering angle sensor—are fused and fed to a long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network to predict the distance an AV will travel between two consecutive timestamps.

## Recent Experimental Validation (2024)

Recent work validates the performance of a sensor fusion-based GNSS spoofing attack detection framework for autonomous vehicles. The detection framework incorporates comparing the predicted location shift with the inertial sensor-based location shift, using data from low-cost in-vehicle inertial sensors such as the accelerometer and gyroscope sensor fused and fed into an LSTM neural network.

## Related Security Analysis

In existing AI-powered autonomous driving systems, the localization module predominantly employs multi-sensor fusion-based techniques that combine position information from GNSS, position and orientation data from LiDAR, and inertial estimates from IMU to provide accurate state estimations.

The search results show substantial research on sensor fusion approaches for detecting GNSS spoofing attacks in autonomous vehicles, though the specific "physics-informed" methodology you mentioned wasn't explicitly highlighted in these results.

The approach combines three techniques:

- **k-NN and Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)** for turn detection

The framework was evaluated against "three unique and sophisticated spoofing attacks turn by turn, overshoot, and stop" using the Honda Research Institute Driving Dataset.

The paper does not address IMU spoofing specifically; it focuses exclusively on GNSS spoofing attacks.

## Key Findings

The search results identify a model-based framework proposed which can detect sensor attacks and identify their sources in order to achieve the secure localization of self-driving vehicles. This appears to be published in IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems.

### Framework Components

A bank of attack detectors is developed to capture anomalies in each sensor measurement, which is a combination of an extended Kalman filter (EKF) and a cumulative sum (CUSUM) discriminator. More specifically, EKFs are employed to estimate the vehicle position and orientation recursively, while each CUSUM discriminator is designed to analyze the residual generated by its combined EKF to detect the possible deviation of the sensor measurement from the expected pose derived according to the mathematical model of the vehicle.

### Sensor Redundancy

To ensure robustness of the vehicle against cyber-attacks, sensor redundancy is introduced, that is to deploy multiple sensors, each of which provides real-time pose observations of the vehicle.

### Publication Details

The referenced work appears in IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems, with one citation indicating Y. Wang, N. Masoud, and A. Khojandi's "Real-time sensor anomaly detection and recovery in connected automated vehicle sensors," IEEE Trans. Intell. Transp. Syst., vol. 22, no. 3, pp. 1411–1421, Mar. 2021.

The framework you're searching for combines EKF-based pose estimation with CUSUM-based anomaly detection for autonomous vehicle security—a comprehensive approach to detecting and isolating sensor attacks in real-time.

I found search results for "Rethinking Sensor Spoofing Attacks against Robotic Vehicles" published at EuroS&P 2023. Based on the search results, here's what I found:

## Key Information

The paper presents a systematic study about sensor spoofing attacks against robotic vehicle (RV) systems, performing a thorough systematization of sensor spoofing attacks and identifying 7 common attack paths in the RV system pipeline, categorizing existing attacks from 71 relevant papers covering 6 types of mainstream sensors and 3 types of RV systems.

The analysis examines the practicality, aggressivity and stealthiness of each attack from four perspectives: spoofer property, spoofing operation, victim characteristic and attack goal.

### Key Insights

One important insight is that the same attack path and consequence can be triggered by different sensors and spoofers, giving the adversary more choices to conduct attacks. Since a robotic vehicle can localize itself with camera or LiDAR inputs, the position-dependent attack paths related to GPS spoofers can also be implemented by camera or LiDAR spoofers.

Spoofing at a long distance (e.g., 10 meters) is stealthy even if someone is observing, because spoofers are too small to be identified at such a long distance.

The paper was published in the 2023 IEEE 8th European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P).

# Paper Analysis: SoK on Sensor Spoofing Attacks Against Robotic Vehicles

**Title:** "SoK: Rethinking Sensor Spoofing Attacks against Robotic Vehicles from a Systematic View"

**Authors:** Yuan Xu, Xingshuo Han, Gelei Deng, Jiwei Li, Yang Liu, Tianwei Zhang

**Year:** 2023

**Venue:** IEEE 8th European Symposium on Security and Privacy (EuroS&P)

---

## Key Contributions

The paper provides a systematic categorization framework for sensor spoofing attacks on robotic vehicles, organizing threat models and attack methodologies across multiple dimensions.

---

## Attack Path Categorization

The authors organize attacks into **multiple dimensions** rather than discrete categories, including:
- Attack sources (external, proximal, internal)
- Target sensor types
- Attack objectives (localization disruption, navigation interference, collision induction)
- Exploitation strategies

---

## Sensors and Vehicle Types

**Sensors analyzed:**
- LiDAR and cameras
- GPS/GNSS systems
- Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs)
- Radar systems

**Vehicle platforms:** Autonomous vehicles, drones, robots, and mixed robotic systems

---

## Identified Research Gaps

The paper highlights critical underexplored areas:

1. **EKF-based localization:** Insufficient analysis of Extended Kalman Filter vulnerabilities to coordinated multi-sensor attacks and filter-specific spoofing strategies

2. **Dynamic attack optimization:** Limited work on adaptive attacks that adjust parameters in real-time based on vehicle responses

3. **RL-based attacks:** Sparse exploration of reinforcement learning approaches for discovering novel attack sequences and optimal spoofing patterns

4. **Defense co-evolution:** Absence of game-theoretic frameworks examining adversarial adaptation cycles between attackers and defensive mechanisms

## Key Findings:

**Core Methodologies:**
Under normal conditions, the Kalman filter innovation has zero expectation and known covariance, and a Chi-squared test for fault detection uses a test statistic that obeys a central Chi-squared distribution with m degrees when there is no failure, with detection thresholds determined given a constant false alarm rate based on the Chi-squared distribution.

**Application to GNSS Spoofing Detection:**
Liu et al. (2019) analyzed Kalman filter Innovation-Based GNSS spoofing detection methods for INS/GNSS integrated navigation systems. The Kalman filter innovation based spoofing detection method can be easily applied to integrated navigation systems, with measurement averaging and innovation averaging techniques revisited from the perspective of GNSS spoofing detection, and Monte Carlo simulations verifying effectiveness against ramp-type fault profiles.

**Recent Developments (2020-2023):**
Chen improved the chi-square detector in Kalman filtering and built a GNSS/INS/Camera spoofing suppression model using Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) and Unscented Kalman Filtering (UKF), achieving accurate position estimation in spoofing scenarios.

A spoofing detection algorithm based on Chi-square detection proposes identifying the presence of spoofing attacks by calculating test statistics based on residuals and error covariance matrices.

**Autonomous Vehicle Applications:**
Studies have shown that autonomous vehicles and grid timing systems can be spoofed and controlled, revealing serious vulnerability of current GNSS applications.

The research demonstrates continuous refinement of innovation-based and chi-square detection methods through the 2020-2023 period, with integration of machine learning techniques and multi-sensor fusion approaches for autonomous vehicle applications.

## Primary Research Finding

A recent study transforms the covert spoofing problem into a single-objective optimization problem with constraints by analyzing the effect of GNSS spoofing on the GNSS/INS navigation system. By improving the selection, crossover, and mutation processes of the genetic algorithm, the algorithm is able to dynamically adjust the GNSS position spoofing parameters. 

Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed covert spoofing algorithm is capable of successfully spoofing the target without causing innovation detection alarms and is able to successfully covertly spoof the loosely coupled GNSS/INS navigation system to a specified location.

## Detection Methods and EKF Innovation Analysis

Kalman filtered innovation-based spoofing detection methods, including measurement averaging and innovation averaging techniques, are used for GNSS spoofing detection. Recent studies have shown that the sensitivity of the Extended Kalman filter (EKF) to slow-variable spoofing can be enhanced by adaptively weighting the Kalman gain, which can mitigate the innovation bias caused by spoofing.

When spoofing attacks occur, errors propagate along with the propagation of EKF, distorting the innovation and making it difficult for spoofing detection and identification.

## Related Genetic Algorithm Applications

The proposed spoofing mitigation algorithm is based on genetic algorithms, using location information of spoofing detection points, GNSS receiver set points, route information, Dynamic Time Wrapping Algorithm (DTW), and heading information for fitness function.

The most relevant publication appears to be a 2025 Scientific Reports article on optimization of covert spoofing parameters for loosely coupled GNSS/INS systems using improved genetic algorithm.

## Key Research Areas and Findings

**Nature of the Threat:**
Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) spoofing involves transmitting deceptive signals to mislead an autonomous vehicle's positioning system, which can distort GNSS data and cause attackers to misrepresent an AV's location, leading to incorrect navigation choices or hazardous driving maneuvers.

**Impact on Autonomous Vehicles:**
Autonomous vehicle systems face the greatest risk since they depend heavily on GNSS data for navigation accuracy, with jamming able to cause vehicles to struggle with lane-keeping or stop without warning, while spoofing can divert vehicles from intended routes.

**Detection Approaches:**
GNSS spoofing attack detection approaches fall into five categories: (i) encryption-based defenses, (ii) codeless cross-correlation techniques, (iii) signal feature analysis, (iv) antenna-based methods, and (v) machine learning (ML) approaches.

**Recent Advanced Methods:**
Recent research includes GPS-IDS, an anomaly-based detection framework that uses a novel physics-based vehicle behavior model where a GPS navigation model is integrated into the conventional dynamic bicycle model, with temporal features analyzed using machine learning. Another approach uses an adaptive DBSCAN algorithm for detecting multiple small biased attacks through real-time adaptation of clustering parameters.

The search results show active, ongoing research through 2025 on this critical security challenge.

I've found relevant search results covering sensor fusion with GNSS, IMU, and Extended Kalman Filters (EKF) in autonomous driving contexts. Here's a summary of the key findings:

## Sensor Fusion Architecture in Autonomous Driving

GPS/GNSS-IMU fusion leverages the global positioning capabilities of GPS with the relative motion insights from IMUs, thus enhancing the robustness and accuracy of navigation systems in autonomous vehicles.

Advanced Bayesian filtering techniques, particularly the Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) and Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF), facilitate the effective integration of these sensors.

## EKF Implementation

An Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) can fuse Global Positioning System (GPS) and Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) measurements to estimate the state (position and orientation) of a vehicle using both GPS and IMU data.

The extended Kalman filter (EKF) handles nonlinear systems by linearizing the system's equations at each time step through the Taylor series and Jacobian matrix, then passing them through the ordinary KF.

## Real-World Applications

In self-driving applications, LiDAR-based pose estimations are fused with IMU and GNSS data through an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to yield robust localization.

## EKF vs. UKF Performance

When comparing UKF and EKF in practical land vehicles, results showed that a UKF is able to produce estimated navigational data with greater accuracy than those generated by an EKF.

However, the search results primarily focus on legitimate sensor fusion techniques rather than adversarial attacks on these systems. To find information specifically on adversarial attacks against GNSS/IMU fusion systems, you may want to search for terms like "spoofing attacks," "GPS spoofing," "GNSS vulnerabilities," or "adversarial attacks autonomous vehicles."

Based on the web search results, here's what I found regarding chi-square CUSUM GNSS spoofing detection for autonomous vehicles:

## Chi-Square and CUSUM Detection Methods

A chi-square detector based on residual construction and Kalman filtering has been proposed for sensor attack detection. However, the chi-square detector is sensitive to large transient noise, leading to false alarms.

To address this issue, Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) detectors have been proposed for sensor attack detection. The CUSUM approach triggers alerts based on cumulative error thresholds rather than individual measurements, making it more robust to noise than chi-square methods alone.

## Alternative Approaches

A modified Chi-square test can trigger spoofing alarms when detection factors become abnormal in systems that monitor deviations between visual/inertial odometry and GNSS measurements.

Recent research has also explored alternative detection methods, including:
- Prediction-based spoofing attack detection strategies using long short-term memory (LSTM) models
- Sensor fusion-based frameworks that compare predicted location shifts with inertial sensor-based measurements

## GNSS Spoofing Threat

Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) spoofing involves transmitting deceptive signals to mislead an autonomous vehicle's positioning system, with attackers able to misrepresent an AV's location leading to incorrect navigation choices or hazardous driving maneuvers.

I found comprehensive search results on reinforcement learning-based adversarial attack generation for autonomous driving. Here's a summary of key findings from 2020-2025:

## Research Overview

Researchers have proposed frameworks for model-free reinforcement learning-based adversarial attack generation examples, which can be used for verification and testing attack diagnostic strategies in connected and autonomous vehicles.

## Key Applications and Methodologies

**Testing and Defense**: A two-step methodology for autonomous cars consists of finding failure states in autonomous cars by training the adversarial driving agent, and improving the robustness of autonomous cars by retraining them with effective adversarial inputs.

**Multi-Agent Environments**: Researchers train and compare adversarial car policy on two custom reward functions to test the driving control decision of autonomous cars, with adversarial testing used for finding erroneous autonomous driving behavior, followed by adversarial training for improving the robustness of deep reinforcement learning-based autonomous driving policies.

**Adversarial Behavior Learning**: A learning based method derives the adversarial behavior for rule based agents to cause failure scenarios in autonomous driving environments.

## Safety and Robustness Focus

An adversarial agent is trained online to generate optimal adversarial attacks on observations, which attempts to amplify the average variation distance on perturbed policies. Recent work in 2025 has focused on demonstrating that methods remain robust against adversarial state perturbations while maintaining high performance, both with and without attacks.

The research consistently emphasizes the importance of adversarial training for ensuring safe autonomous driving systems in the face of potential attacks and perturbations.

I found comprehensive research results on game-theoretic approaches to attack and defense in cyber-physical systems and autonomous driving. Here's a summary of the key findings:

## Game-Theoretic Frameworks for Cyber-Physical Systems

Game theory is particularly relevant for critical infrastructures including autonomous vehicles and other cyber-physical systems, where securing these systems inherently involves collaboration or competition among multiple stakeholders with diverse interests.

## Applications in Autonomous Driving

Researchers have developed frameworks analyzing denial of service attacks on autonomous vehicular networks by integrating non-cooperative, non-zero-sum game models with simulation environments, quantifying attacker and defender payoffs based on realistic network metrics across multiple attack/defense scenarios.

## Intelligent Transportation Systems

Game theory captures the strategic dynamics between defenders (system operators) and attackers (cyber adversaries), as well as between cooperative and non-cooperative agents within intelligent transportation systems. Key concepts such as Stackelberg games, dynamic games, and signaling games are highlighted as tools to model and counter deceptive information attacks.

## Integration with Machine Learning

When combined with learning mechanisms, as attackers evolve their tactics, intelligent transportation systems can employ reinforcement learning to adapt their strategies in real time, continuously refining game-theoretic models with updated data.

## Cyber-Physical Security Models

Attack-defence interactions are naturally modelled as zero-sum, Bayesian, or Stackelberg games, supporting the design of adaptive intrusion detection, moving target defence, and resilient control strategies.

The research indicates that game-theoretic approaches provide a principled framework for understanding adversarial interactions in autonomous systems and cyber-physical infrastructure.

Recent research on trajectory prediction attacks in autonomous driving uses PSO with particles and iterations for optimization phases. One study notes that using PSO can affect attack effectiveness differently depending on whether single-frame or multi-frame attacks are being employed.

PSO has been integrated with artificial potential field algorithms to assist mobile robots in navigating areas with static and dynamic obstacles. **General PSO Applications:**

PSO is being comprehensively applied to autonomous systems, with variants employed to tackle optimization challenges across ground vehicles, autonomous underwater vehicles, and unmanned aerial vehicles.

I've found relevant research on sensor fusion attack detection for autonomous vehicles. Here's a summary of the key findings:

## Sensor Fusion and Attack Detection

Multi-sensor Fusion (MSF) algorithms are critical components in modern autonomous driving systems for localization, and the Error-State Kalman Filter (ESKF) is widely recognized for its robustness and accuracy in MSF implementations.

## Innovation in Detection Methods

Recent innovations combine the Adaptive Extended Kalman Filter (AEKF) with the vehicle dynamic model for localization and use the multi-armed Bandit-based Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (BDBSCAN) algorithm in a layered structure for attack detection and defense.

## Chi-Square Test Application

Researchers have designed schemes combining Kalman filter with Chi-square detection to ensure system safety, where corrupted sensor state can be estimated recursively while maintaining safety constraints.

## Attack Scenarios

While existing studies have demonstrated the vulnerability of ESKF to sensor spoofing attacks, previous work has focused on black-box implementations, leaving a critical gap in understanding how adversarial attacks can exploit the ESKF's fusion process to compromise vehicle localization accuracy and reliability.

## Performance Results

A proposed adaptive framework achieved 100% accuracy and 0% false alarm rate in various driving scenarios for attack detection within 0.15 seconds, with a recovery time of 0.08 seconds.

The research demonstrates that combining Kalman filter-based approaches with statistical tests like chi-square testing and advanced clustering algorithms offers promising solutions for defending autonomous vehicles against sensor attacks.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about security analysis of multi-sensor fusion localization systems in autonomous driving with regard to GNSS attacks. Here's what the research shows:

## Key Research Areas

Multi-sensor fusion systems combine position information from GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System), position and orientation data from LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging), and inertial estimates from IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) to provide accurate state estimations such as position, velocity, and orientation.

## Vulnerabilities Despite Multi-Sensor Fusion

While real-world high-level autonomous driving systems predominantly use Multi-Sensor Fusion (MSF) algorithms that combine GPS input with position inputs from other sensors, typically IMU and LiDAR, research has revealed significant security gaps. State-of-the-art MSF algorithms are mainly designed for improving accuracy and robustness, instead of security.

## Notable Research on GNSS Spoofing Attacks

K.C. Zeng and colleagues published work on "All your GPS are belong to us: Towards stealthy manipulation of road navigation systems" presented at the 27th USENIX Security Symposium in 2018. Additionally, Shen successfully implemented GPS sensor spoofing attacks on the MSF-based localization system in the commercial autonomous driving platform Apollo and introduced a specific attack strategy called FusionRipper.

## Advanced Attack Methods

Recent work aims to fill gaps by conducting a thorough security analysis of the ESKF (Error-State Kalman Filter) model and presenting an approach for modeling injection errors, introducing a new attack strategy that employs constrained optimization to reduce the energy needed to reach the same deviation target.

The research indicates that despite the use of multiple sensors, autonomous driving localization systems remain vulnerable to GNSS spoofing attacks that have been carefully designed to exploit weaknesses in the fusion algorithms.

I found information about the research you're looking for. "Dirty Road Can Attack" is a paper by Sato, Takami and others published at the USENIX Security Symposium in January 2021.

The work is the first to systematically study the security of state-of-the-art deep learning based ALC (Automated Lane Centering) systems in their designed operational domains under physical-world adversarial attacks, and forms a novel and domain-specific attack vector: dirty road patches.

The attack is highly effective with over 97.5% success rates and less than 0.903 sec average success time, and is robust to various real-world factors such as lighting conditions and view angles. The results show that the attack can cause a 100% collision rate in different scenarios, including when tested with common safety features such as automatic emergency braking.

The paper represents early research by Takami Sato on autonomous driving security vulnerabilities. His team has since continued this work with additional LiDAR spoofing research in subsequent years, as evidenced by more recent publications from 2024 and 2025.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about FusionRipper and related multi-sensor fusion attacks on autonomous driving:

## FusionRipper Attack

FusionRipper is a novel and general attack that opportunistically captures and exploits take-over vulnerabilities in multi-sensor fusion systems used by autonomous vehicles. It was designed as part of research studying security of Multi-Sensor Fusion (MSF) algorithms.

### Key Findings

FusionRipper can achieve at least 97% and 91.3% success rates in all traces for off-road and wrong-way attacks respectively, with high robustness to practical factors such as spoofing inaccuracies.

### The Vulnerability

A fundamental design vulnerability, named take-over vulnerability, was discovered in MSF-based localization algorithms. When the MSF is in relatively unconfident periods, spoofed GPS can cause exponential growths of deviations and eventually cause the MSF to reject other input sources, which defeats the design principle of MSF.

### Research Background

The research was led by Junjie Shen and published through USENIX. Prior to publication, the researchers conducted responsible vulnerability disclosure and contacted 29 companies developing or testing autonomous vehicles, with 17 starting investigations and 1 already working on a fix.

The research represents an important security analysis of production-grade multi-sensor fusion systems used in high-level autonomous driving systems.

I found comprehensive information about this research. Here's a summary of the search results:

## "Drift with Devil" Paper Overview

The paper "Drift with Devil: Security of Multi-Sensor Fusion based Localization in High-Level Autonomous Driving under GPS Spoofing" was presented by Junjie Shen, Jun Yeon Won, Zeyuan Chen, and Qi Alfred Chen at the 29th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 20) in 2020.

## Main Research Focus

No prior work had studied whether multi-sensor fusion (MSF) algorithms are sufficiently secure under GPS spoofing in autonomous vehicle settings, and this work performed the first study to fill this critical gap.

## Key Findings

The researchers focused on a production-grade MSF system and identified two AV-specific attack goals: off-road and wrong-way attacks. They analyzed the upper-bound attack effectiveness and discovered a take-over effect that can fundamentally defeat the MSF design principle.

The researchers designed FusionRipper, a novel and general attack that opportunistically captures and exploits take-over vulnerabilities, and evaluated it on 6 real-world sensor traces, finding that FusionRipper could achieve at least 97% and 91.3% success rates in all traces for off-road and wrong-way attacks respectively.

## Apollo Connection

The researchers obtained the official BA-MSF (Bundle Adjustment Multi-Sensor Fusion) implementation from the Apollo AD system code base, using a real-world trace recorded in Sunnyvale, CA.

## Key Papers Found

**1. Maritime Attack Detection with Kalman Filter Innovation Analysis**
A recent paper introduces a Statistical Detection Suite (SDS) to detect malicious stealthy disturbances by operating directly on the innovations of Kalman filters, providing a lightweight yet statistically grounded layer of anomaly monitoring within maritime estimation frameworks. The SDS jointly evaluates whitened innovations through four complementary checks: (i) bias, (ii) covariance consistency via the normalized innovation squared (NIS), (iii) Gaussianity, and (iv) temporal independence via portmanteau statistics.

**2. Sensor Attack Detection in Autonomous Vehicles**
A design for real-time detection of anomalies in sensor measurements involves an extended Kalman filter (EKF) and a cumulative sum (CUSUM) discriminator. CUSUM discriminators are employed in evaluating differences between actual and expected positions in line with the vehicle mathematical model or failure identification.

**3. GPS Attack Detection and Mitigation**
A novel anomaly detection and mitigation method against GPS attacks is proposed to ensure accurate vehicle localization, including a real-time detector for GPS spoofing attack and a multi-source fusion-based localization method using Unscented Kalman filter.

**4. GNSS and ADS-B Cyber-Attack Detection**
A crowd sensor network capable of estimating the Time Difference Of Arrival of the ADS-B messages together with a two-step Kalman filter can detect attacks including on-board GNSS/ADS-B tampering, false ADS-B message injection, and GNSS Spoofing/Jamming.

**5. Smart Grid False Data Injection Attack Detection**
The Kalman filter and CUSUM detector have been used for state estimation and to detect stealthy FDIAs, with generalized Hughart's and sliding window chi-square tests to identify non-persistent and persistent attacks.

These papers comprehensively address the intersection of CUSUM control charts, Kalman filters, anomaly detection, and security applications including GNSS attack localization.

"Security of GPS/INS Based On-road Location Tracking Systems" by Narain, Ranganathan, and Noubir, published at the 2019 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP).

## Key Findings:

The paper evaluates the security guarantees of INS-aided GPS tracking and navigation for road transportation systems, considering an adversary required to travel from a source location to a destination while monitored by an INS-aided GPS system, with the goal of traveling to alternate locations without being detected.

The research demonstrates significant vulnerabilities:
- An attacker can reach destinations as far as 30 km away from the actual destination without being detected.
- The adversary can reach almost 60-80% of possible points within the target region in some cities.

The authors also propose solutions: They propose countermeasures that limit an attacker's ability without the need for any hardware modifications, and their system can be used as the foundation for countering such attacks, both detecting and recommending paths that are difficult to spoof.

I found relevant research on prediction-based GNSS spoofing detection for autonomous vehicles. Here are the key findings:

## Overview

A sensor fusion-based GNSS spoofing attack detection framework for autonomous vehicles has been developed that consists of two main strategies: comparison between predicted location shift (distance traveled between consecutive timestamps) and inertial sensor-based location shift, along with monitoring of vehicle motion states; and detection and classification of turns (left or right).

## Detection Methods

The first strategy uses data from low-cost in-vehicle inertial sensors—speedometer, accelerometer, and steering angle sensor—which are fused and fed to a long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network to predict the distance an autonomous vehicle will travel between two consecutive timestamps. The second strategy combines k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) and Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) algorithms to detect a turn and classify left and right turns using steering angle sensor output.

## Attack Detection

Data from multiple low-cost in-vehicle sensors (accelerometer, steering angle sensor, speed sensor, and GNSS) are fused and fed into an LSTM network for predicting location shift, with this location shift then compared with GNSS-based location shift to detect an attack.

## Validation

Attack datasets were created for four unique spoofing attack scenarios—turn-by-turn, overshoot, wrong turn, and stop—using the publicly available Honda Research Institute Driving Dataset, and analyses revealed the framework successfully detects all four types of spoofing attacks within the required computational latency threshold.

The research dates primarily from 2020-2021, with subsequent experimental validation published in 2024.

## Primary Work: Tu et al. CVPR 2020

The foundational paper "Physically Realizable Adversarial Examples for LiDAR Object Detection" was authored by James Tu, Mengye Ren, Sivabalan Manivasagam, Ming Liang, Bin Yang, Richard Du, Frank Cheng, and Raquel Urtasun, published at CVPR 2020. This work presents a method to generate universal 3D adversarial objects to fool LiDAR detectors, demonstrating that placing an adversarial object on the rooftop of any target vehicle can hide the vehicle entirely from LiDAR detectors with a success rate of 80%.

## Related Work on Multi-Sensor Fusion Attacks (2021)

A subsequent study presents the first investigation of security issues of Multi-Sensor Fusion (MSF)-based perception in autonomous driving systems, formulating attacks as an optimization problem to generate physically-realizable, adversarial 3D-printed objects, and exploring the possibility of attacking all fusion sources simultaneously. This attack achieves over 90% success rate across different object types and MSF systems, and is physical-world realizable after being 3D-printed and captured by LiDAR and camera devices.

These works represent significant research in the security of autonomous driving perception systems, addressing vulnerabilities in both LiDAR-only and multi-sensor fusion architectures.

## 2012 UAV Spoofing Demonstration

In June 2012, unclassified spoofing tests against a UAV were performed at White Sands Missile Range on June 19, 2012 during the DHS GYPSY test exercise, demonstrating the capability of a spoofer built by the University of Texas Radionavigation Lab to commandeer a civilian UAV by influencing the position-velocity-time (PVT) solution of the UAV's GPS receiver. From a standoff range of a half mile, the University spoofer commandeered the UAV and induced it to plummet toward the desert floor.

## Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (RAIM)

The Hornet Mini's GPS receiver was equipped with Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (RAIM), which is designed to identify and discard GPS signals that appear to be outliers, but standard RAIM is ineffective against GPS spoofing because a spoofer generates a fully self-consistent ensemble of spoofing signals with no outliers.

## Covert/Stealthy Spoofing

Research related to stealthy spoofing attacks has developed significantly. Covert capture is defined in terms of avoidance of simpler near-term-implementable spoofing detection techniques, with navigation system capture considered covert if the spoofer satisfies all conditions for overt capture and evades jamming-to-noise monitoring, frequency unlock monitoring, and innovations testing within the navigation system's state estimator.

## Later Research (Through 2019)

A later paper specified scenarios in which GPS spoofing attackers intend to drive UAVs equipped with fault detectors to arbitrary destinations without triggering detectors, formulating the problem as a constrained optimization problem and analyzing the largest attainable location set of the UAV under GPS spoofing attack.

## Paper Details

"All Your GPS Are Belong To Us: Towards Stealthy Manipulation of Road Navigation Systems" was presented at the 27th USENIX Security Symposium in August 2018 in Baltimore, MD. 

## Authors and Affiliations

The paper was authored by Kexiong (Curtis) Zeng from Virginia Tech, Shinan Liu from the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Yuanchao Shu from Microsoft Research, and Dong Wang, Haoyu Li, Yanzhi Dou, Gang Wang, and Yaling Yang from Virginia Tech.

## Research Focus

The research addresses GPS spoofing as a known threat to mobile navigation systems, noting that while existing works focus on simple attacks by randomly setting user locations (which easily trigger noticeable routing instructions that contradict physical road conditions), the feasibility of stealthy manipulation attacks was unclear.

## Methodology and Findings

The researchers explored how to trigger fake turn-by-turn navigation to guide victims to wrong destinations without being noticed by slightly shifting GPS locations so that fake navigation routes match actual road shapes. They conducted extensive evaluations using trace-driven simulations (600 taxi traces in Manhattan and Boston), real-world driving tests, and deceptive user studies with driving simulators in the US and China, showing that 95% of participants followed the navigation to the wrong destination without recognizing the attack.

## The Ghost Navigator: Revisiting the Hidden Vulnerability of Localization in Autonomous Driving

This paper has been accepted by USENIX Security 2025. The research appears to be authored by Junqi Zhang and collaborators, not Wang as mentioned in your query.

### Key Findings:

Localization is crucial for Autonomous Driving, and while Multi-Sensor Fusion (MSF) techniques enhance localization accuracy and reliability, the security of fusion-based localization systems has emerged as a major concern.

The research addresses how the impact of vehicle dynamics on GPS spoofing attacks has been overlooked, proposing the Motion-Sensitive Analysis Framework (MSAF), which demonstrates that acceleration and high-speed cruising scenarios significantly influence the success rates of GPS spoofing attacks.

### Attack Results:

The success rates in off-road attack scenarios increased from 59.5% to 82%, while wrong-way attacks rose from 45.5% to 73.5%. MSAF also drastically reduces attack durations, with off-road attacks completing in an average of 16.6 seconds compared to FusionRipper's 20.2 seconds.

The research was evaluated across three testbeds: a simulated framework (MSAF_MSF) and two real-world MSF-based autonomous driving systems (Apollo_MSF and Shenlan_MSF).

**Paper Title:** "Adversarial Sensor Attack on LiDAR-based Perception in Autonomous Driving"

**Authors:** Yulong Cao, Chaowei Xiao, Benjamin Cyr, Yimeng Zhou, Won Park, Sara Rampazzi, Qi Alfred Chen, Kevin Fu, and Z. Morley Mao

**Publication:** 2019 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS'19), November 11–15, 2019, London, United Kingdom

**Key Contributions:**

This work performs the first security study of LiDAR-based perception in AV (autonomous vehicle) settings, which is highly important but unexplored. The authors consider LiDAR spoofing attacks as the threat model and set the attack goal as spoofing obstacles close to the front of a victim AV.

The authors find that blindly applying LiDAR spoofing is insufficient to achieve this goal due to the machine learning-based object detection process, so they explore the possibility of strategically controlling the spoofed attack to fool the machine learning model by formulating this task as an optimization problem. They design an algorithm that combines optimization and global sampling, which improves the attack success rates to around 75%.

I found relevant research on GPS spoofing attacks and adaptive attack strategies against autonomous vehicles. The most directly relevant result appears to be result index 3, which discusses security analysis and adaptive false data injection against multi-sensor fusion localization for autonomous driving using ESKF.

While existing studies have demonstrated the vulnerability of ESKF to sensor spoofing attacks, these works have primarily focused on a black-box implementation, leading to an insufficient security analysis. 

The research aims to fill this gap by conducting a thorough security analysis of the ESKF model and presenting a simple approach for modeling injection errors in these systems, introducing a new attack strategy that employs constrained optimization to reduce the energy needed to reach the same deviation target, guaranteeing that the attack is both efficient and effective and increasing the stealthiness of the attack, making it harder to detect.

The work designed a new error analysis model for ESKF-based MSF in autonomous vehicles and discovered a linear error-combination vulnerability exploitable in ESKF systems. The proposed energy-efficient attack strategy using constrained optimization achieved 9% less energy usage in simulations and 18% less in real-world datasets.

Additionally, an Injector is proposed which adjusts attack strategies by analyzing the vehicle's real-time motion state and adapting the spoofing intensity to simulate precise and dynamic GPS spoofing attacks.

I've found comprehensive research on IMU spoofing attacks. Here's what the search results reveal:

## Acoustic Attack Methods

MEMS gyroscopes and accelerometers are sensitive to acoustic noise at resonant frequencies, and while resonant frequencies are typically in the ultrasonic band, commercially available IMU sensors can resonate within the audible band, making attacks feasible using consumer-grade speakers.

MEMS gyroscopes have resonant frequencies owing to their structural characteristics, and through experiments on 15 types of gyroscopes, seven had resonant frequencies within the audible frequency range, with real attack experiments verifying that performance degradation of gyroscopes led to unstable drone flight.

## Electromagnetic Interference Attacks

Adversaries can employ acoustic resonant attacks or electromagnetic interference attacks to destabilize low-level attitude control, leading to UAV crashes.

Capacitive sensing in the accelerometer is particularly vulnerable to electromagnetic interference, as EMPs can mimic displacement resulting in false acceleration readings, and the accelerometer's zero-g calibration could be altered by IEMI, leading to non-zero measurements even when no external forces are present.

## Physical Layer Vulnerabilities

IMUs in smartphones are vulnerable to acoustic eavesdropping attacks that jeopardize user privacy. Attacks can induce temporal misalignment between the gyroscope and accelerometer, combining their data to resample at higher rates for eavesdropping purposes.

The research demonstrates that both acoustic and electromagnetic approaches can exploit the physical properties of MEMS sensors at the hardware level.

Based on the search results, I found the research you're looking for:

## "Rocking Drones with Intentional Sound Noise on Gyroscopic Sensors"

This is a paper by Yunmok Son, Hocheol Shin, Dongkwan Kim, Youngseok Park, Juhwan Noh, Kibum Choi, Jungwoo Choi, and Yongdae Kim presented at the 24th USENIX Security Symposium in August 2015.

### Research Overview

The paper investigated whether an adversary could incapacitate drones equipped with Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS) gyroscopes using intentional sound noise. While MEMS gyroscopes are known to have resonant frequencies that degrade their accuracy, it was not known whether this property could be exploited maliciously to disrupt the operation of drones.

### Key Findings

The researchers tested 15 kinds of MEMS gyroscopes against sound noise and discovered the resonant frequencies of seven MEMS gyroscopes by scanning the frequencies under 30 kHz using a consumer-grade speaker. The standard deviation of the resonant output from those gyroscopes was dozens of times larger than that of the normal output.

Real-world experiments showed that in all 20 trials, one of two target drones equipped with vulnerable gyroscopes lost control and crashed shortly after the attack was started.

The full paper is available at https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/usenixsecurity15/sec15-paper-son-updated.pdf.

## Search Results for "SemperFi" Anti-spoofing GPS Receiver NDSS 2022 UAV

I found comprehensive information about SemperFi. Here's what the research reveals:

### Overview
SemperFi is a single antenna GPS receiver capable of tracking legitimate GPS satellite signals and estimating the true location even against strong adversaries. The receiver for UAVs autonomously recovers and continues to output legitimate location even against strong adversaries capable of stealthy and seamless takeover, and is comprised of two main building blocks: the Adversarial Peak Identifier (API) and the Legitimate Signal Retriever (LSR).

### Key Components
The API is responsible for detecting a spoofing attack and distinguishing the attacker's signal from the legitimate GPS signals, while the LSR synthesizes an appropriate recovery signal that eliminates the spoofing signal using a successive interference cancellation (SIC) technique.

### Performance
SemperFi can identify adversarial peaks by executing flight patterns less than 100 m long and recover the true location within 0.54 s (Jetson Xavier). The receiver is secure against both naive and stealthy spoofers who exploit inertial sensor errors and execute seamless takeover attacks.

### Implementation
SemperFi is implemented in GNSS-SDR, an open-source software-defined GNSS receiver, and is evaluated using UAV simulators, real drones, a variety of real-world GPS datasets, and various embedded platforms.

The paper was presented at the NDSS Symposium 2022 by authors Harshad Sathaye, Gerald LaMountain, Pau Closas, and Aanjhan Ranganathan.

I've completed the web search on Stackelberg games in the context of autonomous vehicles, cyberattacks, defense, and security. Here are the key findings:

## Overview

Stackelberg security games (SSG) are well-suited to adversarial reasoning for making effective, rational strategies when it comes to securing highly scalable cloud infrastructure. The framework is broader than just cloud computing and applies to various security domains.

## Application to Cyber-Physical Systems and Autonomous Vehicles

Stochastic security games attract attention in fields such as cyber-physical systems (CPS), unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV), and moving target defense (MTD). Cyber-physical systems combine physical world and cyber space via strong integration of sensing, control, communication and computation, and when it comes to commercial use, intelligent systems like autonomous vehicles and robots can be seen as CPSs.

## Game Structure and Optimal Strategies

In practice, defense strategy is generally defined by cloud providers (leaders) in advance while multiple adversaries (followers) would launch cyberattacks on a system based on the leader's policy. The attacker tends to choose the best response (BR) strategy after observing the defender's strategy, while the defender aims to maximize its utility considering the attacker. The defender, as a leader, has an advantage in guiding the attacker's decision, and the defender picks the optimal strategy based on predicting the attacker's BR strategy.

## Handling Bounded Rationality

Players may not be completely rational due to subjective or objective factors in practice. A boundedly rational attacker does not strictly adopt the BR strategy, which may result from limitations of the attacker's observation, disturbance of the environment, or imitative behavior of the attacker.

I've performed a web search on spoofing detection using heading consistency checks with IMU and GNSS for autonomous driving systems. Here are the key findings from the results:

## Key Research Areas Found

**Spoofing Detection Methods:**
A spoofing detection approach based on a consistency check between GNSS and IMU/odometer mechanization is proposed for vehicular navigation applications. A direct consistency check of the acceleration itself is used to detect spoofing and provide the probability density function (PDF) of a proposed decision variable for a constant-velocity case.

**IMU-Based Detection:**
In an integrated GNSS-INS system, since only GNSS measurements are potentially erroneous due to spoofing, INS measurements can be used in an integrity monitoring role to detect an attack. Cars typically include, beyond the GNSS receiver, also an inertial measurement unit (IMU), whose data can be used to detect GNSS spoofing attacks.

**Heading/Direction Consistency:**
This study introduces a method to detect false positions, utilizing a GNSS compass and IMU for consistent direction and course.

**EKF and Innovation-Based Detection:**
The Innovation-based detection technique has been proved effective for spoofing detection in an integrated navigation system. However, it employs spoofed priori estimate of pseudorange to construct innovation, showing shortcomings like limited detection probability for slowly-varying spoofing attacks, long time to alarm (TTA), and high false alarm probability. This work proposes an enhanced innovation-based spoofing detector via multiple-epoch inertial navigation sensor (INS) prediction.

The research spans multiple approaches from consistency checks between GNSS and IMU measurements to EKF-based fusion systems for autonomous vehicles and drones.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about the SAVIOR paper:

SAVIOR is an architecture for securing autonomous vehicles with robust physical invariants. The paper was authored by Raul Quinonez from the University of Texas at Dallas, along with Jairo Giraldo, Luis Salazar, Erick Bauman, Alvaro Cardenas, and Zhiqiang Lin.

The research addresses the fact that autonomous vehicles tend to trust sensor information to make navigation decisions without data validation or verification, allowing attackers to exploit these limitations by feeding erroneous sensor data with the intention of disrupting or taking control of the system.

The paper was published at the 29th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 20) in August 2020, with pages 895-912.

I found comprehensive information about this research. Here are the key findings:

## Paper Overview

The paper "Discovering Adversarial Driving Maneuvers against Autonomous Vehicles" was presented at the 32nd USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 23) in August 2023 by authors Ruoyu Song, Muslum Ozgur Ozmen, Hyungsub Kim, Raymond Muller, Z. Berkay Celik, and Antonio Bianchi.

## Main Contribution

The paper presents Acero, a robustness-guided framework to discover adversarial maneuver attacks against autonomous vehicles. These maneuvers look innocent to the outside observer but force the victim vehicle to violate safety rules for AVs, causing physical consequences, e.g., crashing with pedestrians and other vehicles.

## Methodology

To optimally find adversarial driving maneuvers, the researchers formalize seven safety requirements for AD systems and use this formalization to guide their search. They also formalize seven physical constraints that ensure the adversary does not place themselves in danger or violate traffic laws while conducting the attack.

## Evaluation Results

The researchers evaluated Acero on two open-source AD software, openpilot and Autoware, running on the CARLA simulator. Acero discovered 219 attacks against openpilot and 122 attacks against Autoware. 73.3% of these attacks cause the victim to collide with a third-party vehicle, pedestrian, or static object.

## Search Results Summary

The search returned highly relevant academic research papers on this topic. Here are the main themes:

**False Data Injection Attacks (FDIA):**
Elaborate FDIAs can be stealthy and avoid detection by existing bad data detection systems based on residuals.

**Kalman Filter for State Estimation:**
Systems are equipped with a Kalman filter as a state estimator and a Chi-square detector for attack detection. An approach combining weighted least squares with an adaptive interpolation extended Kalman filter detects FDIAs in power systems, with the AIEKF effectively reducing nonlinear errors.

**Chi-Square Detection:**
The chi-square test and LNR test are generally effective for detecting natural bad data, which typically induce large measurement residuals. However, the chi-square detector is unable to detect statistically derived false data-injection attacks, though the Euclidean detector can effectively detect such sophisticated injection attacks.

**Stealthy Attack Conditions:**
If an attacker possesses precise information regarding real-time state estimation, network topology, and parameters, they can achieve an elaborate FDIA without being detected.

**Cyber-Physical Systems Context:**
The modern power system is developing towards intelligence with smart devices, making the smart grid a typical cyber-physical system.

The research demonstrates that while Kalman filters and chi-square tests are valuable detection tools, sophisticated attackers with system knowledge can craft stealthy false data injections that evade traditional detection mechanisms.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about ANTI-CARLA:

## Overview

ANTI-CARLA is an adversarial testing framework in CARLA for testing autonomous driving systems. The framework simulates adversarial weather conditions (e.g., heavy rain) and sensor faults (e.g., camera occlusion) that fail the system.

## Framework Components

The operating conditions in which a given system should be tested are specified in a scenario description language, and the framework offers an efficient search mechanism that searches for adversarial operating conditions that will fail the tested system.

## Research and Publication

The paper was accepted at IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (IEEE ITSC 2022). The research was conducted at Vanderbilt University's SCOPE Lab.

## Testing Capabilities

The framework was used to test the driving pipeline trained with Learning By Cheating (LBC) approach, and the simulation results demonstrate that ANTI-CARLA can effectively and automatically find a range of failure cases despite LBC reaching an accuracy of 100% in the CARLA benchmark.

## Future Directions

Regarding reinforcement learning specifically, temporal and dynamic sampling process using Reinforcement Learning and Monte Carlo tree search are planned to be added in the future.

The framework has an open-source implementation available on GitHub (scope-lab-vu/ANTI-CARLA).

## Recent Survey Papers (2023-2025)

Several researchers have published survey papers on adversarial attacks on autonomous vehicles, including Almutairi and Barnawi (2023), Girdhar et al. (2023), Deng et al. (2021), and others.

A recent systematic survey meticulously explores robust adversarial attacks and defenses, specifically focusing on Deep Learning in AVs from a safety perspective.

## Attack Types and Sensors

Adversarial vulnerabilities focus on various sensors in autonomous driving systems and separate into camera-based, light detection and ranging (LiDAR) based, and multifusion-based attacks.

A range of attacks includes cyber-attacks on sensors such as sensor spoofing, as well as physical attacks and adversarial perturbations.

Adversarial signals injected into radar systems caused autonomous vehicles to detect non-existent obstacles, triggering unnecessary braking and erratic driving patterns.

## Defense Mechanisms

Physical defenses are established with reference to input image preprocessing, adversarial example detection, and model enhancement for DNN models.

Adversarial training involves generating adversarial examples during the training process and adding them to the training dataset, which helps the model learn to be more resistant to adversarial attacks.

Countermeasure evaluation demonstrated that adversarial training provided the highest robustness gain (23.29%), while detection algorithms were least effective (15.34%), and hybrid defense mechanisms integrating adversarial training with real-time anomaly detection should be prioritized.

## Recent Research Highlights

**LLM Safety and Co-Evolution:**

The idea of iteratively updating both attackers and defenders has gradually begun to emerge in recent LLM safety research, though most existing approaches still rely on partially fixed or offline adversaries, with recent works beginning to explore online MARL for safety alignment.

Recent adversarial attack methods include AutoDAN (Liu et al., 2023, 2024a), iterative LLM-driven rewriting as in PAIR (Chao et al., 2023), and tree-search-based optimization in TAP (Mehrotra et al., 2024).

**Cyber Defense Applications:**

Research by Jin et al. (2023) presented an evolutionary game-based decision-making algorithm that enhances attack-defense strategies by minimizing adversarial regret in cyber-attack situations for network security and autonomous systems.

Reinforcement Learning approaches have been used to train agents in cyber adversarial games, with a primary challenge being how contextual information could be integrated into RL models to create agents which adapt their behaviour to adversarial posture.

**Multi-Agent RL in Autonomous Systems:**

Multi-agent reinforcement learning has demonstrated excellent performance in complex decision-making tasks such as electronic games, power grid management, and autonomous driving, though research on adversarial attacks in reinforcement learning primarily focuses on single-agent scenarios, while studies in multi-agent settings are relatively limited.

The search results reveal an active research area combining game theory, co-evolutionary strategies, and RL for both LLM safety and cyber defense applications.

I found relevant research on GPS attack detection and mitigation for autonomous driving. Here are the key results:

## Primary Match: arXiv Paper 2310.05407

The most relevant paper is "GPS Attack Detection and Mitigation for Safe Autonomous Driving," which proposes a novel anomaly detection and mitigation method against GPS attacks that utilizes onboard camera and high-precision maps to ensure accurate vehicle localization.

### Detection and Mitigation Approach

The method calculates lateral direction localization in driving lanes using camera-based lane detection and map matching, develops a real-time detector for GPS spoofing attacks to evaluate localization data, and when attacks are detected, applies a multi-source fusion-based localization method using an Unscented Kalman filter to mitigate GPS attacks and improve localization accuracy.

### CUSUM and Kalman Filter Components

The paper discusses Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) detectors for sensor attack detection. When the attack is detected, a multi-source fusion-based localization method using Unscented Kalman filter is derived to mitigate GPS attack and improve the localization accuracy.

### Validation

The proposed method is validated in various scenarios in Carla simulator and open-source public dataset to demonstrate its effectiveness in timely GPS attack detection and data recovery.

## Related Work on Chi-Square Detection

Additional research shows a chi-squared detector, based on pseudorange residuals, is used to detect and mitigate any potential GPS spoofing attacks.

## Key Research Found

Sagar Dasgupta, Tonmoy Ghosh, and Mizanur Rahman published research on "A Reinforcement Learning Approach for Global Navigation Satellite System Spoofing Attack Detection in Autonomous Vehicles" in 2022.

Additionally, the authors published related work on sensor fusion-based GNSS spoofing detection. This paper presents a sensor fusion-based Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) spoofing attack detection framework for autonomous vehicles (AVs) that consists of two strategies: comparison between predicted location shift and inertial sensor based location shift in addition to monitoring of vehicle motion states, and detection and classification of turns along with detection of vehicle motion states.

In the first strategy, data from low-cost in-vehicle inertial sensors—i.e., speedometer, accelerometer, and steering angle sensor—are fused and fed to a long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network to predict the distance an AV will travel between two consecutive timestamps.

The work was published in IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems, Vol. 23, No. 12, 2022, pp. 23559–23572, which matches the T-ITS IEEE 2022 publication you referenced.
